title: Bread from Heaven
summary: A month after leaving Egypt, the Israelites in the Desert of Sin grumble that they will starve. The LORD sends quail in the evening and, every morning, a fine flaky food the people call manna, with instructions to gather only a day's portion, except for a double portion before the Sabbath. Some disobey and the hoarded manna rots, but the Sabbath portion keeps; a jar of manna is preserved for later generations, and Israel eats it for forty years.
story: At the sea God rescued Israel from Pharaoh; at Marah (chapter 15) he turned bitter water sweet. Now the wilderness asks a harder question: can God be trusted not just for one great rescue but for every day's food? The people's complaint ("If only we had died by the LORD's hand in the land of Egypt") shows how quickly slavery can look like security. God answers not with rebuke first but with bread, and with a daily discipline that trains his people to trust him. The chapter also introduces the Sabbath before the law is given at Sinai, as a gift to be received rather than a rule to be obeyed. The manna will last until Israel reaches Canaan (Joshua 5:12), so this chapter sets the terms for the whole wilderness period that runs through Numbers.
historical:
The date is given precisely: the fifteenth day of the second month, one month after the exodus (12:2, 12:18). The Desert of Sin (a place name, unrelated to the English word sin) lay between Elim and Mount Sinai, somewhere in the Sinai Peninsula; its exact location depends on where one places Sinai, which is itself debated. The date of the exodus, as noted at chapter 13, is contested.

Two natural phenomena of Sinai have been compared with this account. Quail migrate across the peninsula in spring and autumn, and exhausted flocks can come down in great numbers where they land. And certain scale insects feeding on tamarisk trees in Sinai produce a sweet, sticky secretion that hardens into small white drops in the cool of the morning, which local people have gathered and call by the Arabic word man. Some readers see God's provision working through such means; others note that the biblical manna differs in important ways (its quantity, its appearing six days and not the seventh, its spoiling overnight except on the Sabbath) and treat it as a miracle beyond natural explanation. The text itself presents it as food from God, whatever means he used.
cultural:
Bread was the staple food of the ancient Near East, and the memory of Egypt's "pots of meat" reflects the fact that even slaves on royal projects were fed rations. In the desert, a large group would have had no reliable food at all. The instructions about gathering assume a camp life of tents, households, and daily chores. An omer was a dry measure, here explained as a tenth of an ephah; ancient measures are hard to fix, but it is usually estimated at roughly two liters, a generous day's portion per person.

The Sabbath appears here for the first time as a command to Israel, though Genesis 2:2-3 already tells of God resting on the seventh day. A regular day of rest for everyone, slaves included, was unusual in the ancient world. People who had just come out of forced labor, where work never stopped, are now given a day on which they are forbidden to work, and God provides the food for it in advance. The "Testimony" in verse 34 refers to the tablets of the covenant kept in the ark, which have not yet been given at this point in the story; the verse looks ahead to a later practice, and Hebrews 9:4 describes a golden jar of manna kept with the ark.
literary: The chapter repeats a small set of words: grumbling (again and again in verses 2-12), gathering, morning and evening, and seeing and knowing. The grumbling section (verses 1-12) builds to the appearance of God's glory in the cloud, and the people are told that their complaints are really against the LORD. The name manna comes from the people's question, "What is it?" (in Hebrew, man hu), a play on words the narrator explains in verse 31. The narrative is structured as a test, as God says in verse 4, and the test has two parts: gathering only enough for the day, and not gathering on the seventh. Some fail each part, and the story records both failures without softening them. The closing verses (32-36) step outside the story's time, looking forward to the jar kept for future generations and to the forty years of manna, which shows that the chapter was written to teach later readers as well as to record an event.

outline.t: Grumbling in the Desert of Sin
The LORD promises bread and meat, and his glory appears
Quail and manna, enough for each day
The Sabbath portion and the Sabbath rest

doctrines.note: God feeds his people day by day, in a place where they cannot feed themselves. The manna teaches that daily dependence on God is not a failure of planning but the shape of life with him.

The Sabbath is introduced here before Sinai, as a gift tied to God's provision: he gives the extra food so that his people can rest. Obedience in this chapter is a matter of trusting that God's instruction is good.

The manna tests whether Israel will follow God's word when hoarding seems safer and gathering on the Sabbath seems prudent. Faith here is practical trust expressed in ordinary habits of work and rest.

words.note: Man, manna. The name comes from the question "What is it?" in verse 15 (man hu), so the food is named after the people's bewilderment. It becomes the Bible's great image of bread given from heaven (Psalm 78:24; John 6:31).

Telunnah, grumbling or murmuring. It is a key word of the wilderness stories (see Numbers 14 and 17). Moses tells the people that their grumbling is not against him and Aaron but against the LORD, making clear that complaint about God's leaders was complaint about God's care.

Shabbat, Sabbath, from a root meaning to cease or stop. Its first appearance as a noun in the Bible is here. The Sabbath is presented as "a holy Sabbath to the LORD" and as something "the LORD has given you", a gift before it is a law.

Kavod, glory, from a root meaning heavy or weighty. The glory of the LORD appears in the cloud as he answers the people's complaint. In Exodus, God's glory is his visible presence, which later fills the tabernacle (40:34).

christ: Jesus himself interprets this chapter. After feeding a crowd in John 6, he is told that the fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and he answers that it was not Moses who gave them bread from heaven but his Father who gives the true bread from heaven, and then he says, "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35). He contrasts the manna, which the ancestors ate and still died, with himself, the bread that gives eternal life (John 6:49-51). When tempted in the wilderness Jesus quoted Deuteronomy 8:3, which draws the lesson of the manna: man does not live by bread alone but by every word of God (Matthew 4:4). The prayer he taught his disciples, asking for daily bread, echoes the daily gathering of this chapter, and Paul cites verse 18 to encourage generous sharing among churches (2 Corinthians 8:15).

hard.q: Was the manna a natural substance or a miracle?
hard.a: Some readers point to the sweet secretion found on Sinai tamarisks and to the autumn and spring migrations of quail, and see God's provision working through the natural world he made, as the east wind worked at the sea. Others note that the natural substance appears only in small amounts and only in certain seasons, while Exodus describes enough food for the whole people every day for forty years, a double portion on the sixth day, none on the seventh, and spoiling that stops on the Sabbath. They conclude that the text describes a miracle that no natural product explains. A third group of scholars treats the account as a later tradition that turned a desert food into a symbol of God's care. The chapter's own interest is plain: whatever the means, the food came from God, and it came in a way that taught Israel to trust him one day at a time.

questions: The Israelites remembered Egypt's pots of meat and forgot the slavery. What do you remember selectively when present hardship makes the past look better?
God gave enough for each day and no more. What would it look like for you to trust God for today's needs rather than trying to secure tomorrow's?
The first Sabbath was a gift of rest to former slaves. How do you receive rest, and what makes it hard to stop working?
